sections.label: 1. Words and pictures introduce story meaning
sections.final_normalized_text: 1. Words and pictures introduce story meaningRead the words and look at the illustration together. Each can give information the other does not. Name the clue before explaining what it suggests.ExampleThe worksheet words say, “Mae read.” The picture shows an open book and shelves of books. Together, the words and picture help us imagine the moment.Worksheet picture: the open book and bookshelves add clues about action and place.Try it: What place do the shelves of books suggest? What do the words tell Mae is doing?See answer and explanationThe shelves suggest a library. The words tell us Mae is reading. Point to the visible book and shelves; the picture does not establish every detail about her feelings.

sections.label: 2. Character clues and story animals
sections.final_normalized_text: 2. Character clues and story animalsNotice what a character does and says. These choices can help us understand the character. Pictures may add expression, posture or action clues.ExampleTwo children share crayons in the worksheet picture. A story could say, “Lea passed a crayon to her friend.” The action can suggest kindness.Look at what the children do, not only their faces.Try it: Which action in the picture could suggest kindness? Explain.See answer and explanationPassing or sharing a crayon can suggest kindness because it helps another child join in. Point to the action. Accept a supported interpretation; one smile does not prove every feeling.

sections.label: 3. Setting: where and when
sections.final_normalized_text: 3. Setting: where and whenFind words and image details that show where or when events happen. Explain how they help you picture the place.Example“At night, Jo stood on the beach.” Beach names the place and at night tells when. The worksheet illustration adds a shoreline and a moon.Find the shoreline and moon in this worksheet illustration.Try it: Which word names the place? Which word helps tell when?See answer and explanationBeach names the place; at night tells when. The moon and shoreline are matching picture clues. The picture alone does not tell Jo’s name or an exact clock time.

sections.label: 4. Events and story sequence
sections.final_normalized_text: 4. Events and story sequenceFollow what happens first, next and last. Words such as then and pictures of changes can help us connect events.Example“A gust blew the hat away. Then Sam caught it. Sam put it back on.” Gust means a short burst of wind.Try it: What happens between the hat blowing away and Sam putting it on?See answer and explanationSam catches it. Explain the change using the supplied sequence. An event is something that happens; the setting names where or when it happens.

sections.label: 5. Picture clues add to the words
sections.final_normalized_text: 5. Picture clues add to the wordsAsk what an illustration adds: a place, a movement, an expression or a detail. A picture can also create a playful mismatch with the words.ExampleThe words say, “Mae read.” The picture also shows shelves of books and a plant. These visible details are not named in the short sentence.Words: “Mae read.” What extra detail can you see?Try it: Name one detail the picture adds that the words “Mae read” leave out.See answer and explanationThe bookshelves suggest the place is a library; a plant is another added detail. Point to the visible clue. The picture alone does not tell the book’s title or what Mae is thinking.

sections.label: 6. Compare stories and illustrators respectfully
sections.final_normalized_text: 6. Compare stories and illustrators respectfullyRead books by First Nations Australian creators, other Australian creators and world creators. Compare a specific choice in their words or pictures. Stories and artistic styles can differ within each group.ExampleIn two picture books shared by an adult, find a page where a character helps someone. Compare the action words and one visible picture clue.Try it: Tell a partner one way the two pages build a helpful character.See answer and explanationThe child points to actual words and picture details in each book and discusses what they suggest. Record the title, author and illustrator. Do not label a generic animal picture as First Nations literature or invent cultural meanings.Prepare three actual illustrated booksAdult supplies lawful illustrated copies of Little Bird’s Day by Sally Morgan and Johnny Warrkatja Malibirr, Time for Bed by Mem Fox and Jane Dyer, and Dear Zoo by Rod Campbell, or verified equivalent selections across First Nations Australian, other Australian and world creators. The published text and artwork are not included. Identify author and illustrator; read the whole books and show the actual spreads. Follow publisher/community guidance; do not guess cultural symbolism or imitate artwork.Discuss the actual choices, then compareLittle Bird’s Day: compare an opening daytime spread with a later night spread; explain how real words and visible details create setting and connected events. Time for Bed: hear a returning word pattern and discuss what an actual image adds about the animals or care. Dear Zoo: inspect a real closed and opened flap, listen to the actual describing word and explain the reveal; check any event-order link in the copy rather than testing an unverified animal sequence. Compare one genuine word or image choice from two books and explain its effect. Use all three creator contexts over time; a creator-name quiz is not a substitute. Accept different supported responses and note the help used.

sections.label: 1. Make a relevant connection
sections.final_normalized_text: 1. Make a relevant connectionFirst name a detail from the text. Link it with a safe experience of your own. A useful connection helps explain your response, rather than just matching a colour or object.ExampleOriginal mini-story: “Nia waited for the swing. At last it was her turn. She grinned.” A reader might say, “I waited for a turn at a game. I felt glad when my turn came.”Try it: Which link helps us understand Nia: waiting for a turn at a game, or owning a green pencil? Why?See answer and explanationWaiting for a turn connects the experience. The pencil does not explain this event. A child’s own relevant experience may be different from the model; no one memory is required.

sections.label: 2. Notice story details first
sections.final_normalized_text: 2. Notice story details firstAsk a question about the character, place or event. Check the answer in the text before making a connection. Keep the story detail and your own memory separate.ExampleIn Nia’s mini-story, “At last it was her turn” tells us she gets a turn. It does not say how many children were waiting.Try it: Did Nia get a turn? What words tell us? What could you ask about the event?See answer and explanationYes: “At last it was her turn.” A relevant question might be “What did Nia do when her turn came?” If the answer is not supplied, say we do not know. A memory cannot prove an unstated story fact.Complete story for this discussionOriginal mini-story: “Nia waited for the swing. At last it was her turn. She grinned.” For the comparison, the reader waits for a turn at a game. Keep the shared experience and differing activities clear.

sections.label: 3. Compare with care
sections.final_normalized_text: 3. Compare with careYour experience can be similar without being identical. Explain both the shared part and a difference. Your feelings do not replace the character’s feelings.ExampleNia waits for a swing. The reader waits for a game. Both wait for a turn, but the activities differ.Try it: Name one thing that is alike and one thing that differs in those experiences.See answer and explanationAlike: waiting for a turn. Different: a swing versus a game. Accept another accurate comparison. Do not require identical places, objects or feelings.Complete story for this discussionOriginal mini-story: “Nia waited for the swing. At last it was her turn. She grinned.” For the comparison, the reader waits for a turn at a game. Keep the shared experience and differing activities clear.

sections.label: 4. Use a connection to understand
sections.final_normalized_text: 4. Use a connection to understandExplain how the memory helps you respond to the character or event. Use because to make the link clear.Example“I understand Nia’s glad feeling because I remember finally getting a turn.” That adds an explanation to the connection.Try it: Finish using a safe memory of your own: “I understand waiting because …”.See answer and explanationAccept a relevant, voluntary memory and an explanation of its link. If the child has no matching experience or prefers not to share, discuss an imagined example for participation and revisit a safe own-experience connection later; the imagined example is not proof of personal experience.

sections.label: 5. Keep the response relevant
sections.final_normalized_text: 5. Keep the response relevantA response can be different from someone else’s. Point to what in the poem or story prompted it. A drawing or role-play can help you explain.ExampleOriginal mini-poem: “Rain on the roof. Rain on my shoe. I hop in a puddle. What will you do?” One reader remembers enjoying puddles; another remembers keeping their socks dry.Try it: Which line could you draw or act out? Then explain your own response to that part.See answer and explanationFor example, draw hopping in a puddle and name the matching line. Accept a different feeling or preference with a relevant connection. The speaker saying I is the voice in the poem; it is not automatically the author. Drawing without an explanation does not show the full discussion skill.

sections.label: 6. Share responses respectfully
sections.final_normalized_text: 6. Share responses respectfullyThink first, then share with a partner. Listen to their response, ask a related question or add a connected idea. You can disagree respectfully.Example“You liked the puddle part. I felt worried about wet socks because mine got wet once. What did you like about the puddle?”Try it: Discuss the rain poem with a partner. Add one related response or question after listening.See answer and explanationObserve the actual exchange. Look for a text detail, a safe own-experience link and a response to the partner. Accept speech, signing, AAC or supported communication. Do not score agreement or private disclosure.The complete poem for partner talkOriginal mini-poem: “Rain on the roof. Rain on my shoe. I hop in a puddle. What will you do?” Read the actual lines together before sharing responses.

sections.label: Check learning and offer support
sections.final_normalized_text: Check learning and offer supportWatch for this: A retell alone is not a personal response. Your memory does not change the text. Similar does not mean identical, and readers do not have to agree.Check: Choose a part of a short story or poem. Share a safe connection to your own experience and explain your response. Listen to a partner and ask or answer a related question.See answer and explanationObserve an accurate text detail, a relevant voluntary own-experience link and actual discussion. A worksheet selection alone cannot establish discussion; an imagined example supports participation but does not confirm an own-experience connection.Help: Read a short complete text aloud and offer “In the story … I remember … This helps me understand …”. sections.label: 1. Find the setting
sections.final_normalized_text: 1. Find the setting The setting tells us where and when a story happens. Read or hear the whole short story first. Then find the place and time clues. Sometimes a story gives only one of them; say what you know without filling in missing details.Read togetherAfter lunch, Ruby waited beside the school gate. A tiny dragon landed on her bag. Ruby held out a biscuit, and the dragon nibbled it.Work it throughAsk “Where?” The words beside the school gate tell the place.Ask “When?” After lunch tells the time; an exact clock time is not needed.Check realistic or imagined details. A school gate is familiar, but a tiny dragon makes this an imagined story. Try it together: Name the setting. Does “Ruby” tell us who or where? What makes the story imagined?See answer and explanationThe setting is beside the school gate, after lunch. Ruby is a character: her name answers who. The tiny dragon is the imagined detail. The text gives no season or exact clock time. Watch for this: A character’s name is not a place. “Ruby waited” is an event, not the whole setting. Ask where and when separately. Listen and look for: The child points to or repeats each relevant clue and can distinguish a familiar place from the imagined creature. On paper: Continue with Practice A in the matching worksheet pack. Model first, reduce help as the child is ready, and revisit this focus before the separate test.

sections.label: 2. Know story features
sections.final_normalized_text: 2. Know story features Character asks who is involved. Setting asks where and when. Plot asks what happens and how the events connect. A story map helps keep these questions apart; it is a way to talk about a story, not a requirement to write a new one.Read togetherAt the library on Saturday morning, Finn found a dropped book. He gave it to the librarian. She thanked him.Work it throughRead the complete story. Name the participants: Finn and the librarian.Find the place and time: the library, Saturday morning.Follow the events: Finn finds the book, gives it to the librarian, then receives thanks. Try it together: Put “the library”, “Finn” and “gave the book to the librarian” under who, where or what happened.See answer and explanationWho: Finn. Where: the library. What happened: Finn gave the book to the librarian. “Saturday morning” adds when. The book is an object in this story, not a speaking or acting character.Our story mapWho?Where and when?What happens?Finn and the librarianThe library, Saturday morningA dropped book is found and returned; the librarian thanks Finn. Watch for this: A book or animal can be a character in an imagined story, but every named object is not automatically a character. Check its role in the actual text. Listen and look for: The child sorts details by the question each heading asks and explains one choice. On paper: Continue with Practice B in the matching worksheet pack. Model first, reduce help as the child is ready, and revisit this focus before the separate test.

sections.label: 3. Find the problem
sections.final_normalized_text: 3. Find the problem In many stories a character wants something, but an obstacle gets in the way. That is a problem. A solution is an action that addresses it. Some stories describe connected events without a problem; do not force one into every text.Read togetherLila wanted to water the seedlings. The watering can had a hole, so the water leaked out. Dad brought a jug. Lila used it to water the seedlings.Work it throughFind the goal: Lila wants to water the seedlings.Find what stops her: water leaks from the can.Connect the solution to the problem: a jug holds the water so she can pour it onto the seedlings. Try it together: Would moving the leaky can to another shelf solve the problem? Why does the jug help?See answer and explanationMoving the can does not stop the leak or water the seedlings. The jug can hold the water and lets Lila finish the job. Name how the action helps rather than choosing any event near the ending.Another kind of story: “Zoe picked a flower, put it in a jar and placed the jar on the table.” These events form a short sequence. No problem is stated. Watch for this: The problem is the leak, not the garden setting. A different action is a solution only if it addresses what went wrong. Listen and look for: The child links the goal, obstacle and helping action, using “because” or an equivalent explanation. On paper: Continue with Practice C in the matching worksheet pack. Model first, reduce help as the child is ready, and revisit this focus before the separate test.

sections.label: 4. Follow plot order
sections.final_normalized_text: 4. Follow plot order Track the main events in the order they happen. Words such as first, next and finally can help, but actions also give clues: a result usually follows the action that causes it. Keep a retell faithful to the story.Read togetherMilo put soil in a pot. He planted a seed in the soil. Then he watered it.Work it throughIdentify the starting action: Milo puts soil in the pot.Find what depends on it: the seed is planted in that soil.Place watering after planting, as the story states. Tell the sequence as first, next and finally. Try it together: A retell says, “First he watered the planted seed. Next he put soil in the pot. Finally he planted the seed.” Repair it. Which action belongs in the middle?See answer and explanationFirst he puts soil in the pot; next he plants the seed; finally he waters it. Planting is the middle action. The faulty retell puts watering a planted seed before that seed is planted. Use this story’s clues; do not claim plants can only ever be watered in one order. Watch for this: The order of mixed cards is not the story order. Reread the whole text and connect each action to what must already have happened. Listen and look for: The child orders three events, spots the reversed retell and explains a dependency rather than only naming a sequence word. On paper: Continue with Practice D in the matching worksheet pack. Model first, reduce help as the child is ready, and revisit this focus before the separate test.

sections.label: 5. Notice character choices
sections.final_normalized_text: 5. Notice character choices What a character does and says can suggest a feeling or quality. Say “may feel” when the text leaves room for more than one interpretation. Give the clue. One action does not tell us everything about a person.Read togetherWhen the class game began, Hana noticed a child standing alone. “You can join our team,” she said, and moved over to make space.Work it throughFind the action: Hana makes space.Find the speech: she invites the child to join.Connect them to an idea: this choice is welcoming because it includes someone standing alone. Try it together: What might Hana’s choice suggest? Which words or action support your idea? Do we know for certain how the other child feels?See answer and explanationHana’s choice may suggest kindness or friendliness: she invites the child and makes space. Other supported descriptions are welcome. We do not know the other child’s feeling for certain; the story does not state a reaction. Watch for this: Do not use a face, name or favourite colour as proof of a trait. Return to the stated action or speech. Separate a possible feeling from a fact. Listen and look for: The child offers an interpretation and a matching clue, and accepts another sensible interpretation when its evidence fits. On paper: Continue with Practice E in the matching worksheet pack. Model first, reduce help as the child is ready, and revisit this focus before the separate test.

sections.label: 6. Link story features
sections.final_normalized_text: 6. Link story features Talk about characters, setting and plot together. Ask how a place, time or character choice affects the next event. Compare what is alike and different in two complete short texts before extending to a shared tale or fable.Read togetherOriginal story: Rain began at the playground. Ari put the chalk under the shelter so the drawings could continue there.Original narrative poem:Rain on the street,Wet little feet.Bea finds a doorway,A dry place to stay.Work it throughName who and where in each text: Ari at a playground; Bea on a street. No time of day is stated.Find the shared situation: rain affects what each character does.Compare the actions and outcomes: Ari moves chalk under shelter; Bea finds a dry doorway. The poem uses short lines and rhyme, but both texts tell connected events. Try it together: How does the rain affect the plot in each text? What is similar, and what is different?See answer and explanationIn both, rain leads to seeking shelter. Ari acts to keep a drawing activity going; Bea acts to find a dry place. The characters, places and exact actions differ. The poem’s street/feet rhyme is a form difference; it does not replace discussing the events.Shared-reading follow-up: Choose an age-appropriate complete traditional tale or fable from a lawful, attributed source. Compare its characters, place/time and event pattern with another familiar story. Ask whether a problem is stated and how its ending follows the earlier events. Watch for this: A comparison needs both texts. “They are the same” is too broad; name a shared feature and a difference, with clues. Listen and look for: The child discusses a connection between setting and action, refers to each text and responds to a partner’s question. On paper: Continue with Practice F in the matching worksheet pack. Model first, reduce help as the child is ready, and revisit this focus before the separate test.

sections.label: Teaching help: model, support and check
sections.final_normalized_text: Teaching help: model, support and checkStart: Read a complete short story aloud. Ask the child to tell what happened before separating its features. Use three cards headed who, where/when and what happened; no special materials are needed.Support: Offer two choices, reread the clue and accept pointing, speech, signing, AAC, drawing or adult scribing. Note the help given. Reading and spelling difficulty should not hide an understanding of story features.Core: Ask the child to name a feature and show the clue. Invite a short explanation of how an action affects the next event.Extend within Year 1: Compare two familiar texts, repair a retell or discuss two possible feelings using different clues. Do not require formal plot terminology or a full written story.Partner talk: Think first, share one idea, then ask or answer “Which part tells you that?” Listen for a relevant reply. A paper answer alone cannot show participation in a real discussion.

sections.label: Quick check: discuss a fresh story
sections.final_normalized_text: Quick check: discuss a fresh storyOriginal story: Before breakfast, Mae took her puppy into the yard. The puppy’s ball rolled behind a box. Mae moved the box and the puppy picked up its ball.Who is involved? Where and when?What goes wrong, and which action addresses it?Tell the three main events in order. Explain how Mae’s choice affects the ending.Ask a partner a question about one story feature and respond to their reply.See answer and explanationMae and her puppy are the characters. The setting is the yard, before breakfast. The ball rolls behind a box; Mae moves the box so the puppy can retrieve it. A useful three-event retell is: the ball rolls behind the box, Mae moves the box, the puppy picks up the ball. Taking the puppy into the yard introduces the scene and can also be included. Accept a faithful longer retell. Observe the actual partner exchange and the evidence used.Continue or revisit: Continue when the child distinguishes the features, gives relevant clues and discusses how events connect. If who/where are mixed, return to focus 2. If the retell is reversed, model focus 4 again. If a feeling is guessed without evidence, return to focus 5. Use another fresh story after support; this short check is not whole-year certification.

sections.final_normalized_text: See the idea: Separate who, where and what happens Separate who, where and what happens Character: Sam; Setting: The park; Plot event: Sam lost a ball.. Explain how the event follows losing the ball. An adult can read the directions, model the idea and accept an oral, pointed or drawn explanation where appropriate. sections.label: 1. Hear alliteration
sections.final_normalized_text: 1. Hear alliteration Alliteration repeats a beginning sound in nearby words. Say the words aloud before looking at their spelling. Read the whole short line for meaning, then listen to its pattern.Listen togetherBusy bees buzz beside the bucket.Work it throughRead the line naturally and talk about the bees.Say busy, bees, buzz, beside and bucket slowly. Hear /b/ at the beginning of each.Echo the line and gently emphasise /b/. The repeated beginning sound makes the words sound connected. Try it together: Which keeps the /b/ pattern: “bouncy bear” or “bouncy fox”? Say your choice, then add another familiar /b/ word.See answer and explanation“Bouncy bear” repeats /b/. “Bouncy fox” changes to /f/ in fox. A new phrase such as “bouncy brown bear” is one possible creation; accept another meaningful phrase with the heard /b/ pattern.Adult-led contrast: Say cat and kite. Both begin with /k/ although the letters differ. This is a listening example; the child need not spell either word. Watch for this: A matching first letter is a useful clue, but the sound decides. Introduce spelling exceptions only with adult modelling, not as an independent reading trap. Listen and look for: The child hears the shared sound, echoes the phrase and creates a meaningful new phrase. On paper: Continue with Practice A in the matching worksheet pack. Model first, reduce help as the child is ready, and revisit this focus before the separate test.

sections.label: 2. Hear rhyme
sections.final_normalized_text: 2. Hear rhyme Rhyming words have matching spoken endings, such as cat and hat. Listen from the vowel sound to the end. Naming a picture clearly matters: a picture could have more than one sensible name. Adults should agree on the intended word before asking for a rhyme.Listen togetherThe cat sits on a mat.It watches a little hat.Work it throughListen to the whole two-line rhyme. Name what the cat does.Say mat and hat slowly. Their /at/ endings match, while the beginning sounds differ.Say cat and cup. They start alike, but their endings do not rhyme. Try it together: Say boat, goat and book. Which word does not rhyme? Now listen: “A goat climbs into a boat on the pond.” Complete “The goat is in the ___” using boat or coat so it matches that scene, then reread for meaning.See answer and explanationBook does not rhyme with boat/goat. Boat gives the sensible line “The goat is in the boat.” Coat rhymes too, but it does not match the stated scene of a goat in a boat on the pond. In a different imagined scene a goat could wear a coat; a rhyme must fit the context we are completing. Watch for this: Rhyme is heard, not decided by the last letter. Repeating the exact same word is repetition; for this rhyme task, find a different word with the matching ending. Listen and look for: The child names the words, compares endings, rejects the odd ending and checks the completed line’s meaning. On paper: Continue with Practice B in the matching worksheet pack. Model first, reduce help as the child is ready, and revisit this focus before the separate test.

sections.label: 3. Hear sound words
sections.final_normalized_text: 3. Hear sound words A sound word helps us imagine a noise. Use familiar words such as drip, buzz or bang in a short poem or chant. How we say the word can change the effect; explain why a voice choice fits.Listen togetherDrip, drip, rain on the tin.Soft little drops are tapping in.Work it throughListen once and picture the rain.Find drip: it suggests the sound of drops. Rain names what is falling; it is not itself the sound word in this line.Say drip softly, then more loudly. Compare how the two deliveries make the rain seem. Try it together: Which delivery fits the “soft little drops”: a gentle drip or a shouted DRIP? Echo your choice and explain.See answer and explanationA gentle drip usually fits soft little drops. A loud version could suggest heavier rain or a deliberately different effect. Accept a choice when the child explains it using the text; loud does not automatically mean better. Watch for this: A sound word and an object name ask different things. Model the noise, then return to the whole line so this stays a literary listening activity. Listen and look for: The child imitates the sound word and connects a delivery choice to a detail in the poem. On paper: Continue with Practice C in the matching worksheet pack. Model first, reduce help as the child is ready, and revisit this focus before the separate test.

sections.label: 4. Hear repetition
sections.final_normalized_text: 4. Hear repetition Repetition uses a word or line again. A repeated refrain can help listeners predict and join in. Rhyme matches endings in different words; repetition brings back the same word or phrase. A text can use both.Listen togetherTap with me, tap with me.Tap your knees, tap with me.Work it throughAn adult says both lines once; the child listens for what returns.Point out “tap with me” in both lines. Echo that phrase together.Read again and pause before the final phrase so the child can join in. Keep a comfortable pace. Try it together: Keep the repeated phrase and invent a new line about tapping toes. Is “me” repeated, or is it a new rhyming word?See answer and explanationOne possible line is “Tap your toes, tap with me.” The repeated phrase is kept while the action changes. Me is the same word again, so that example is repetition; it does not supply a new rhyming word. Watch for this: A repeated starting sound, a repeated whole word and a rhyme are different patterns. Say exactly which part returns rather than calling every repetition a rhyme. Listen and look for: The child joins the refrain after listening and changes one action while preserving the repeated phrase. On paper: Continue with Practice D in the matching worksheet pack. Model first, reduce help as the child is ready, and revisit this focus before the separate test.

sections.label: 5. Perform for effect
sections.final_normalized_text: 5. Perform for effect Listen, echo and then perform. We can change pace, volume, clear word endings and optional actions to suit a poem, chant or song. A beat is a steady pulse; word syllables do not always match one beat each. Keep movement comfortable and optional.Listen, echo and performOriginal chant: Hop, hop, stop!Original song words: We can play, come this way.Work it throughSay the chant first. Echo it and tap a steady pulse together. Compare a gentle version and an excited version.For the song, an adult sings the six words to the short original tune below. Let the child listen first, then echo each phrase.Discuss how the sung version differs from the spoken chant. Sing or say the words again so play/way endings can be heard. Try it together: Echo the chant and the song. Choose a calm or lively delivery. What pattern do you hear, and how does your delivery fit?See answer and explanationHop repeats in the chant; hop/stop rhyme. Play/way rhyme in the song. A calm delivery might use a gentler voice and slower pace; a lively delivery might use a brighter voice and brisker pace. There is no single best performance: listen for a deliberate choice and an explanation.Adult tune guide: Use a comfortable pitch. Sing We–can–play to do–re–mi, then come–this–way to mi–re–do. Give each word one steady beat. This is an original short teaching tune; notation is adult support, not a Year 1 assessment. Model it before expecting an echo. Children may join through voice, signing, AAC, tapping or another accessible mode. Watch for this: Talking about a performance is not the same as doing it. Hear a real adult song model and observe the child’s response. Do not require perfect pitch, movement or formal musical notation. Listen and look for: Actual listening, echoing, joining or an accessible response; clear audible patterns and a reason for one performance choice. On paper: Continue with Practice E in the matching worksheet pack. Model first, reduce help as the child is ready, and revisit this focus before the separate test.

sections.label: 6. Invent sound patterns
sections.final_normalized_text: 6. Invent sound patterns Start with a heard model, change it and check your new version. Choose rhyme, alliteration or a repeated refrain. Say your creation aloud: it should keep the chosen pattern and make the meaning you intend. Adult scribing can record the child’s words.Invent and shareRhyme model: A dog sits on a log.Alliteration model: Small snails slide.Work it throughHear dog/log, then collect another familiar rhyming pair such as boat/goat. Make a new meaningful line from that pair.Hear /s/ in small/snails/slide. Change or add a word that keeps the shared beginning sound.Say the new version to a partner. Point out or explain the part that matches, then listen to the partner’s response. Try it together: Invent a short rhyme or alliterative line. Then change one word in the chant from focus 4, or invent new words to the tune from focus 5. Share what you kept and what you changed.See answer and explanationExamples include “A goat floats in a boat” (goat/boat rhyme) and “Small snails sleep” (the /s/ sound returns). “Tap your toes, tap with me” keeps the refrain; “We can go, watch us grow” can use the six-note tune and go/grow rhyme. These are models, not required answers. Accept a different meaningful creation with an audible pattern. Watch for this: A copied line shows imitation; an original change provides evidence of invention. A rhyming word must also fit the intended meaning. Support planning without supplying the whole response. Listen and look for: The child produces a genuine change or new line, performs or communicates it, names or indicates the pattern, and discusses it with someone. On paper: Continue with Practice F in the matching worksheet pack. Model first, reduce help as the child is ready, and revisit this focus before the separate test. The refrain and tune for this new versionOriginal refrain from focus 4: “Tap with me, tap with me. Tap your knees, tap with me.” Original song from focus 5: “We can play, come this way.” Adult sings We–can–play to do–re–mi, then come–this–way to mi–re–do, one word per steady beat at a comfortable pitch. Let the child actually hear the model before inventing new words. These are supplied original teaching models, not traditional cultural works.

sections.label: Quick check: hear it, make it, share it
sections.final_normalized_text: Quick check: hear it, make it, share itOriginal two-line model:Little lizards lie in the sun.Run to the shade when the day is done.Listen to an adult read both lines. Choose a new familiar pair of rhyming words.Invent a short line using alliteration or rhyme, then share it with a partner.Tell your partner what pattern you used and respond to a question or comment.See answer and explanationLittle/lizards/lie share /l/. Sun/done rhyme in usual Australian English despite different spelling; model pronunciation and respect the child’s accent. An original /l/ phrase such as “Little lambs leap” or a meaningful line with another rhyming pair can meet the creation task. There is no single correct invented line. Observe the actual echo, original change and exchange; do not infer them from a written answer.Continue or revisit: If beginnings and endings are mixed, contrast cat/cup with cat/hat aloud. If a copied line is offered for invention, help change one meaningful word. If the pattern works but the meaning is unclear, ask the child to explain their imagined scene or revise the line. Use a fresh example after support.

Work through the exampleBig, blue and bag begin with the same /b/ sound: this is alliteration.Bee and tree have matching ending sounds: they rhyme.Say a short pattern aloud, then choose new words that keep its sound pattern and meaning. sections.label: 1. Choose key events
sections.final_normalized_text: 1. Choose key eventsListen to the whole story more than once until it is familiar. Choose the events someone needs to understand what happened. You can use your own words; you do not need to repeat every sentence.Read togetherSam took a red ball to the park. The ball rolled under a bench. Sam could not reach it. His friend Jo used a stick to roll it out. Sam thanked Jo, and they played together.Work it throughSam took the ball to the park → the ball rolled under a bench → Jo helped get it back → they played together. The red colour is a detail; the lost ball and Jo’s help explain the story.Try it together: Can we leave out Jo’s help and still explain how Sam got the ball back?See answer and teaching guidanceNo. Jo’s help connects the problem to the ending. The ball’s colour can be left out in a short retelling.Watch for this: A list of objects is not a retelling. Ask “What happened?”On paper: Practice A has 10 questions. Use the separate test after teaching and practice; observe an oral retelling or adaptation as well.

sections.label: 2. Use story structure
sections.final_normalized_text: 2. Use story structureA beginning introduces who and where. The middle tells what happens, including a problem if there is one. The ending tells how the story finishes. Not every familiar text has the same pattern.Beginning, middle, endBeginning: Sam and his ball are at the park. Middle: the ball rolls away, and Jo helps. End: Sam thanks Jo, and they play.Work it throughDraw one picture for each part. Point to each picture while you tell the story aloud. The pictures help you remember; your telling gives the listener meaning.Try it together: Which part tells us how the problem is solved?See answer and teaching guidanceThe middle includes Jo using a stick to get the ball back. The ending shows what happens afterwards: Sam thanks Jo, and they play.Watch for this: Do not stop at the problem. Give the listener a clear finish.On paper: Practice B has 10 questions. Use the separate test after teaching and practice; observe an oral retelling or adaptation as well.

sections.label: 3. Keep events in order
sections.final_normalized_text: 3. Keep events in orderTell the events in the order they happen. First, next, then and last can help. Use the story’s meaning as well as these words; adding “first” does not make a mixed-up event correct.Put the events togetherJo got the ball back. Sam took the ball to the park. The ball rolled under a bench.Work it throughStart with Sam taking the ball to the park. Next the ball rolls under the bench. Then Jo gets it back. The help comes after the problem.Try it together: Tell the three events in order. Why does Jo’s help come later?See answer and teaching guidanceSam takes the ball to the park; it rolls under a bench; Jo gets it back. Jo helps because the ball is stuck. A drawing can support the telling.Watch for this: Order the events, not just the cards. Ask why one event follows another.On paper: Practice C has 10 questions. Use the separate test after teaching and practice; observe an oral retelling or adaptation as well.

sections.label: 4. Keep characters and setting clear
sections.final_normalized_text: 4. Keep characters and setting clearName who is involved and where the important events happen. Use actions and speech from the story to show what a character does or feels. Make it clear who “he”, “she” or “they” means.Who did what?Sam could not reach the ball. Jo used a stick to roll it out. “Thank you, Jo,” said Sam.Work it throughJo is the friend who helps. Sam thanks Jo. Their actions and speech show help and gratitude. The story happens at the park; we are not told an exact time.Try it together: Who uses the stick? Tell it clearly without saying only “he did it”.See answer and teaching guidanceJo uses the stick to get the ball. Use Jo’s name when the listener might not know who a pronoun means. Accept an oral character description such as “Jo helps Sam.”Watch for this: Do not invent character actions or feelings for an accurate retelling. Use clues, and distinguish a reasonable inference from a stated fact.On paper: Practice D has 10 questions. Use the separate test after teaching and practice; observe an oral retelling or adaptation as well.

sections.label: 5. Use story language
sections.final_normalized_text: 5. Use story languageUse familiar story words, clear action words and a little character speech. You can act, draw or use a recording to support your telling. A grown-up may write your words for you.Tell and act“I cannot reach it,” said Sam. Jo rolled the ball out. “Thank you,” said Sam.Work it throughPractise Sam’s worried voice, then his thankful voice. Keep the main meaning even if your exact words change. A description like “Jo is helpful” needs an action clue: Jo gets the ball back.Try it together: Say Sam’s words in your own way. What does Jo do that shows help?See answer and teaching guidanceFor example: “It is too far away!” Jo uses a stick to get the ball. Accept different clear wording, gesture and character expression; do not demand memorised lines or a particular accent.Watch for this: Using your own words is still a retelling. Writing accuracy is not the speaking goal.On paper: Practice E has 10 questions. Use the separate test after teaching and practice; observe an oral retelling or adaptation as well.

sections.label: 6. Adapt without losing sense
sections.final_normalized_text: 6. Adapt without losing senseAn adaptation changes part of a familiar story on purpose. Say what you will change. Keep enough familiar characters, events or structure for someone to recognise the story, and make the changed parts fit.Make one deliberate changeChange the place from the park to the classroom. Sam’s ball rolls under a desk. Jo uses a ruler to roll it out. Sam thanks Jo.Work it throughThe place changes, so the bench becomes a desk and the tool becomes a ruler. The familiar problem, help and thankful ending stay connected. You can also change a character or ending; one change is a manageable starting point, not a rule for every adaptation.Try it together: Could the ball roll under a classroom desk and then be rescued from a park bench with no explanation? Tell a version that fits.See answer and teaching guidanceThat version mixes places without explaining the move. Keep it in the classroom: the ball rolls under a desk, Jo helps get it back, and Sam thanks Jo. Accept other coherent adaptations with an explained link.Watch for this: A forgotten event is not automatically a deliberate adaptation. Ask what was changed and whether the new story makes sense.On paper: Practice F has 10 questions. Use the separate test after teaching and practice; observe an oral retelling or adaptation as well.

sections.label: 1. Find a text purpose
sections.final_normalized_text: 1. Find a text purposeA text is a message made with words, pictures or both. Its purpose is its job: it might tell a story, share facts, give steps, invite someone or encourage a choice. Read the message, not just its topic.Read two texts about a kiteText A: “Jo took her kite to the park. The wind lifted it high.” Text B: “A kite has a frame and a tail.”Work it throughA tells events involving Jo: it tells a story. B shares information about a kite. The topic is the same, but the texts do different jobs. A story can be invented or based on real events.Try it together: Which text helps us learn what a kite has? Give a clue.See answer and teaching guidanceB. The frame and tail are information about a kite. Accept a spoken, signed or supported explanation using this detail.Watch for this: An animal or object in a text does not make it a fact text. Ask what the whole message does.On paper: Practice A has 10 questions. Teach and practise first, then use the separate test.

sections.label: 2. Use instruction clues
sections.final_normalized_text: 2. Use instruction cluesInstructions tell someone what to do. A title may name the task. A list can tell what is needed. Doing words such as fold and draw tell the actions; numbered steps can show their order.Make a name cardYou need: paper and a pencil. 1. Fold the paper. 2. Write your name. 3. Stand the card on the table.Work it throughThe list names the materials. The steps show the actions in order. The whole text helps someone make a name card. A picture of a folded card could help show how to do the first step.Try it together: What do the numbers help the reader do? How is the materials list different?See answer and teaching guidanceThe numbers help the reader follow the order. The list tells what is needed; it does not give the method.Watch for this: Numbers can organise a story too. Check whether the words tell the reader to act or describe events.On paper: Practice B has 10 questions. Teach and practise first, then use the separate test.

sections.label: 3. Use information clues
sections.final_normalized_text: 3. Use information cluesAn information text helps a reader learn or find something out. A heading names a topic, a label names a part, and a contents list can show where to find a topic. Facts and useful details support the text’s job.Find a topicContents: Birds — page 2; Frogs — page 5. On the bird page, a picture label says “magpie” and the sentence says “Birds have feathers.”Work it throughThe contents list points to the bird page. The label names the pictured bird. The sentence shares a fact. Each feature helps readers find or understand information.magpie — Birds have feathers.Try it together: Where would you look for frog information? What does a picture label do?See answer and teaching guidanceStart on page 5. A label names the pictured object, animal or part. Accept an explanation that links the feature with its use.Watch for this: “I like frogs best” tells a liking, not a fact about frogs. Do not treat every sentence about an animal as factual information.On paper: Practice C has 10 questions. Teach and practise first, then use the separate test.

sections.label: 4. Use persuasion clues
sections.final_normalized_text: 4. Use persuasion cluesSome texts try to make us choose or do something. Look for the request and a reason supporting it. A request tells what the writer wants; a reason explains why someone might do it.A class request“Please choose the shady park for our class walk. We can rest in the shade.”Work it throughThe writer wants the class to choose the shady park. Resting in the shade is the reason. The words encourage a choice rather than give a walking route.Try it together: Name the request and its reason. Would “Our class went to the park” have the same job?See answer and teaching guidanceRequest: choose the shady park. Reason: we can rest in the shade. “Our class went to the park” reports an event; it does not ask the reader to choose.Watch for this: A poster can give information, warn or persuade. Its size, bright colour or the word “please” alone does not prove its purpose.On paper: Practice D has 10 questions. Teach and practise first, then use the separate test.

sections.label: 5. Use invitation clues
sections.final_normalized_text: 5. Use invitation cluesAn invitation asks people to come to an event. It usually tells what is happening, when it happens and where to go. These details help the invited people plan.Come to a class show“Come to our class show! Friday at 2 pm. School hall.”Work it through“Come” invites readers. “Class show” tells what; “Friday at 2 pm” tells when; “school hall” tells where. A factual note about halls would have a different purpose.Try it together: The invitation says “Come to our show on Friday” but gives no place. What needs adding, and why?See answer and teaching guidanceAdd where the show is, for example “in the school hall”. Guests need to know where to go. Other event details may also need checking.Watch for this: An attractive picture cannot replace missing event details. Read the message to check that people can actually attend.On paper: Practice E has 10 questions. Teach and practise first, then use the separate test.

sections.label: 6. Explain with evidence
sections.final_normalized_text: 6. Explain with evidenceTell someone the text’s job and point to a useful clue. Compare the whole messages. Suggest a plan that considers both ideas.See answer and teaching guidanceFor example, “We could sit together in the quiet corner.” Accept a feasible plan that connects both contributions. sections.label: 1. Recognise imaginative texts
sections.final_normalized_text: 1. Recognise imaginative textsAn imaginative text can tell an invented story. It can include things that could happen, or fantasy things that could not happen. Look for a character and events, and use what you know about the whole text.A realistic invented storyThe writer made this story up: “Ari lost her hat at the oval. She searched beside the gate and found it.”Work it throughAri is a character. Losing, searching and finding are story events. The events could happen, but the writer invented them. A story does not need magic.Try it together: A writer invents a story about a child catching a bus. Must it be an information report because buses are real?See answer and teaching guidanceNo. A real place or possible event can appear in an invented story. Use the writer’s context and the whole message, rather than calling every possible event a fact.Watch for this: An impossible event is a useful fantasy clue. A possible event alone does not prove that a text gives factual information.

sections.label: 2. Recognise informative texts
sections.final_normalized_text: 2. Recognise informative textsAn informative text helps us learn or find something out. A heading can name the topic, labels can name parts, and sentences can give facts or useful details. Check what the words actually explain.Find the information you needCard A: “Wombats dig burrows in the ground.” Card B: “Wally the wombat packed a bag and set off on a journey.”Work it throughA gives information about real wombats. B follows a character’s story events. Both mention wombats, but only A answers where wombats make their homes.Try it together: Which card would you choose to find out where wombats live? Point to the useful words.See answer and teaching guidanceChoose A. “Burrows in the ground” answers the question. Accept an oral or supported explanation pointing to that detail.Watch for this: A photograph or heading can be a clue, but it does not prove the text’s purpose. Stories and persuasive messages can also have photographs.

sections.label: 3. Recognise persuasive texts
sections.final_normalized_text: 3. Recognise persuasive textsA persuasive text tries to influence what someone chooses, thinks or does. Find the request or opinion, then a reason supporting it. Ask what the writer wants from the reader.A request and its reason“Choose the shady seat. It will keep our lunch out of the sun.”Work it throughThe request is to choose the shady seat. Keeping lunch out of the sun is the reason. The message encourages a choice; it does not tell a character’s adventure.Try it together: What is the request? Which words explain why the reader might agree?See answer and teaching guidanceRequest: choose the shady seat. Reason: keep our lunch out of the sun. A suitable paraphrase is accepted.Watch for this: “Please” alone is not proof of persuasion. Read the full message. Facts can support a persuasive request.

sections.label: 4. Find similarities
sections.final_normalized_text: 4. Find similaritiesA similarity is something that is the same. Texts can share a topic, a word, a fact, an action or a picture while doing different jobs. Say what both texts actually include.A shared fact, different jobsA: “Birds have feathers.” B: “Please keep the bird’s feathers clean so it can stay healthy.”Work it throughBoth mention a bird’s feathers. A gives information; B asks for an action. Their shared topic does not make their purposes the same.Try it together: A story says “Jo watered the garden.” A message says “Water the garden so the plants can grow.” What do both mention?See answer and teaching guidanceBoth mention watering a garden. One tells Jo’s event; the other encourages the reader to water. Do not claim both are instructions or both are stories.Watch for this: Name a specific similarity supported by both texts. Do not guess a shared detail that appears in only one.

sections.label: 5. Explain differences
sections.final_normalized_text: 5. Explain differencesA difference is something that is not the same. Compare what the messages do, what their words tell us and how they organise ideas. Use “Both …, but …” to connect a similarity with a difference.Same picture, different messagesTwo cards show the same garden picture. A says “Plants need water.” B says “Please water our plants so they do not dry out.”Work it throughThe picture and topic are the same. A shares information. B uses information to support a request. The words reveal a purpose difference that the picture alone cannot show.Try it together: What is the same? What does B ask the reader to do that A does not?See answer and teaching guidanceBoth concern plants and water. B asks the reader to water the plants. A gives information without that request. Accept a reasoned explanation of overlapping information and persuasion.Watch for this: Do not use “It has a picture” as the difference when both cards have pictures. Check both messages.Two actual cards with the same pictureCard A: “Plants need water.”Card B: “Please water our plants so they do not dry out.”

sections.label: 6. Use evidence and choose a text

sections.label: Teach each strand: model, practise and check
sections.final_normalized_text: Teach each strand: model, practise and check Choose a short text with letter–sound patterns the child has been taught. Explain unfamiliar vocabulary before reading. A decodable text practises those patterns; an authentic text has a real purpose, such as a classroom notice or a book. An adult may support unfamiliar words in an authentic text. 1. Blend sounds in orderPoint to shop. Say /sh/ /o/ /p/, then blend the sounds into the whole word. The two letters sh work together to represent one sound.Try: Read fish. Which two letters work together?Answer and teaching guidancesh represents one sound. Blend /f/ /i/ /sh/. If the child names letters without blending, model the sounds and slide them together. 2. Read meaningful phrasesRead The little dog / ran home. The slash shows a useful phrase group for practice; it is not printed punctuation. First solve unfamiliar words, then reread the words together so the sentence sounds like speech.Check: Who ran home? Listen for the child keeping The little dog together. Answer: the little dog. 3. Let punctuation guide your voiceRead Can the dog jump? as a question. Read Stop! with an urgent voice, without shouting. A full stop marks the end of a sentence; take a natural pause before the next sentence.Try: Read The dog can jump. and Can the dog jump? aloud. Listen for the child distinguishing a statement from a question. 4. Check all the lettersThe printed word is frog. If you say flag, compare the middle letters: r and o. Read /f/ /r/ /o/ /g/, then blend. Check the beginning, middle and end; a first letter alone does not identify a word.Read the printed sentence: “The frog hops.” Use the letters to read frog; the picture helps show what frog means. 5. Check grammar and meaning after decodingThe printed sentence is The dog runs. A reader says The dog run. Return to runs, notice the final s, and reread. The spelling tells you the word; the sentence helps you check that it sounds right and makes sense.Try: You read The dog jumps. as The dog bumps. Both words can be words, but the printed word starts with j. Return to the letters instead of choosing a word that merely seems plausible. 6. Reread for fluencyRead The fish swims. First read accurately, then reread in a meaningful phrase. Explain what the fish does. Fluency includes accuracy, suitable pace and expression; racing through a sentence is not the goal.Adult check: Listen to both readings. Notice whether the child keeps the words correct, groups them smoothly and explains that the fish swims. Give brief help, then invite another reading. High-frequency words and asking for helpPractise familiar words such as the and is in short sentences. Use the known letter–sound parts and explicitly teach any unusual part. If blending and rereading still do not resolve a word, the child can ask an adult for help, then read the sentence again. Support, core and extendSupport: model one word, blend together and echo-read a short phrase.Core: read a short taught-pattern text, correct a mismatch and reread with meaning.Extend: reread a slightly longer familiar text or an adult-supported classroom notice, keeping accurate words, phrasing and meaning. Exit checkListen to the child read The fish swims. Ask them to explain what the fish does, check the letters after an error, and reread the sentence smoothly. Expect /f/ /i/ /sh/, the correct printed words and an explanation of swimming. Reteach the particular sound or word that caused difficulty before trying again.

sections.label: Common misconceptions
sections.final_normalized_text: Common misconceptionsOnly guessing from context — Look at the letters and sounds.Sounding without meaning — After decoding, check the sentence makes sense.Robot reading — Practise phrase groups, not one word at a time forever.

sections.label: Try these
sections.final_normalized_text: Try theseBlend and check — Read a decodable word, then use it in a sentence.ship → The ship sails.Phrase scoop — Mark small phrase groups and re-read smoothly.The little dog / ran home.Meaning monitor — Stop when reading sounds wrong and fix it.Does it make sense?

sections.label: Explain and apply
sections.final_normalized_text: Explain and applyBlend and check meaningRead: The frog sat on a log. Which two words rhyme? Read their letters first, then explain how the sentence helps you check the meaning.Answer and teaching guidanceFrog and log rhyme. Read their printed letters and blend first; the sentence then helps you check the meaning. A rhyming guess alone does not identify a printed word.Use phonics firstYou see the word shop. Which sounds help you read it?Answer and teaching guidanceThe digraph sh and the sounds /o/ and /p/ help the reader blend the word.Read in phrasesWhere is a good pause: The little dog / ran home or The / little dog ran home?Answer and teaching guidanceThe little dog / ran home keeps words in meaningful phrases and supports fluency.Self-correctThe printed sentence is “The frog hops.” You accidentally read “The flag hops.” What should you do?Printed words: “The frog hops.” Check the letters in frog.Answer and teaching guidanceStop and return to the printed letters. Blend the sounds to check the word, then reread and check meaning; do not guess the word from the picture.

sections.label: Check your understanding
sections.final_normalized_text: Check your understandingQuick checksWhat should you do if a word does not make sense?Blend: sh-o-p.Why re-read a sentence?What is phrasing?I am ready when I canI can recognise many high-frequency words while reading.I can use phonics, phrasing, context and grammar together to keep meaning.I can self-correct or ask for help when the text stops making sense.

sections.label: 1. Visualise the details
sections.final_normalized_text: 1. Visualise the detailsVisualising means making a picture in your mind from the words. Keep the objects, actions and places that the text actually names.Read: A child reads an open book at a table.Use the picture to practise noticing details, then visualise a new sentence.Work through it: Picture the child, the open book and the table. A closed book would change a stated detail. Your drawing can be simple; the important part is its meaning.Try it: A dog curls up on a soft mat. Describe or draw what you picture. Which details came from the words?Check the answerInclude a dog, curled up, on a soft mat. The words do not give its colour, so more than one drawing is possible. Do not score artistic quality.

sections.label: 2. Predict, then check
sections.final_normalized_text: 2. Predict, then checkA prediction is an idea about what might happen or what a text might be about. Use the title, picture or words as a clue. Read more to keep or change your idea.The pile and brooms are clues. They do not tell us exactly what happens next.Before reading on: What might the children do with the leaves? Say “I think … because …”. Record your first prediction before opening the next part.Read the next part and checkThe children put the leaves in a garden bin.Did you keep or change your prediction? Explain using this new information. Putting leaves in a bin was a sensible prediction, but the picture alone did not guarantee it.Try it with words: Dark clouds filled the sky. Mia took an umbrella. What may happen next?Check the answerIt may rain. The clouds and umbrella support this idea; they do not prove rain will fall.Try it with a book: Use an adult-supplied book. Look at its title and cover, make a prediction, then pause during reading to check it.

sections.label: 3. Connect and infer
sections.final_normalized_text: 3. Connect and inferA connection links a text with something you have experienced, learnt or imagined. Explain the shared part, rather than naming an unrelated memory.The child supplies food that a garden bird can eat.Model a connection: “This reminds me of leaving water for birds. Both give birds something they need.”Try it: What does this picture remind you of? Say how the two situations are connected. A known or imagined example is fine.Check the answerAccept any relevant connection with an explanation, such as feeding a pet or helping wildlife. A learner does not need to disclose a personal experience.An inference uses a clue plus what you know to work out something the words do not state directly.Read: Max smiled after opening a gift. Max probably felt pleased: his smile is the clue, and we know people often smile when pleased.Try it: Sam packed a raincoat. Why might Sam have packed it?Check the answerSam may expect rain or want to stay dry. A raincoat is used in wet weather. The text does not prove it will rain; other sensible explanations are possible.

sections.label: 4. Find the main idea and summarise
sections.final_normalized_text: 4. Find the main idea and summariseThe main idea tells what the whole text or picture is mostly about. A summary keeps the important ideas or events and leaves out small details.Read: Mo had a flat tyre. Mum helped fix it. Mo rode again.Model: “Mo gets help to fix a tyre and rides again.” This keeps the problem, help and result. “Mo has a tyre” leaves out the main events.Try it: Beetles have six legs. Their hard wing covers protect their wings. Many beetles have spots. What is this text mostly about?Check the answerFeatures of beetles. This covers the legs, wing covers and possible spots. “Spots” alone is just one detail.Retell a story: Use a familiar adult-supplied book. Briefly say the important beginning, what happens, and how it ends. You do not need to repeat every sentence.

sections.label: 5. Ask questions and find evidence
sections.final_normalized_text: 5. Ask questions and find evidenceAsk questions that help you understand. Check whether an answer is stated, can be inferred with a clue, or is not given.Read: Kim puts a pear in a lunchbox.What does Kim pack? A pear. Point to “pear”.Who eats it? These words do not say.Try it: Ruby put her bag under the bench. Ask a question that these words answer, then show the evidence.Check the answerFor example: “Where did Ruby put her bag?” Answer: under the bench. The words “under the bench” are the evidence. Accept another accurate question and answer.Listen for informationAdult reads aloud: “A garden bird eats seeds. It drinks water from a shallow dish.” Ask the learner what the bird eats and where it drinks. Read twice if needed without pointing out the answers.Check the answerSeeds; from a shallow dish. Accept two distinct accurate details. Record listening as the response route.Use vocabulary and contextRead: A path was slick after rain. It was easy to slip.“Easy to slip” helps explain that slick means slippery here. Use the sentence around an unfamiliar word, then check that your meaning fits.Try it: The towel was damp after the splash, but it was not dripping. What does damp mean here? Which words help?Check the answerA little wet. The splash and “not dripping” help distinguish this from completely dry or soaking wet. Let the learner use the clues before defining the word.

sections.label: Quick check: explain your thinking
sections.final_normalized_text: Quick check: explain your thinkingUse these short checks with listening, viewing or reading. An adult may read the text aloud.Picture this: “Two kittens sit under a bench.” Name the details you must keep.“Lee put a finished book in a bag for the library.” What might Lee do next? Give a clue.“Ava’s smile faded when her ice block fell.” How might Ava feel? Explain.“Jo spilled some pencils. Jo picked them up and put them in a pot.” Give a short summary.“A bird built a nest in a tree.” Ask a question the words answer. Can they tell you how much the nest cost?Check the answer1. Two kittens, sitting, under a bench. 2. Lee may return the book; it is finished and the bag is for the library. 3. Ava may feel sad or disappointed; the lost treat and fading smile are clues. 4. Jo tidies up the spilled pencils. 5. For example, “Where did the bird build its nest?”—in a tree. The words give no price. Accept equivalent answers supported by the details.If an answer is uncertain, revisit the matching focus. Use the learner’s explanation to choose the next teaching step.
